title: Euphoria and oversizing after wins
teaches: A winning run breeds overconfidence: you credit the wins to your skill, treat profit as house money and want to size up. Keep the risk your plan set before the run. Change it only by a rule you wrote while calm, and grade each trade by the decision, not the result.

facts.quote: Overconfidence bias is a cognitive bias in which individuals tend to overestimate their abilities, knowledge, and skills in a particular area.
facts.claim: Overconfidence bias is overrating your own ability, knowledge and skill.

facts.quote: Overconfidence bias is the tendency to overestimate your abilities when it comes to money matters, tricking your brain into making risky bets, disregarding data, and believing it's possible to consistently beat the market.
facts.claim: Schwab: overconfidence is overrating your abilities with money, and it leads to risky bets and ignored data.

facts.quote: A wealth of easily accessible online information, anecdotal evidence, or simple luck in random investments may encourage you to make risky decisions.
facts.claim: Plain luck on a few investments can push you toward risky decisions.

facts.quote: The danger of overconfidence is that it can lead people to take larger positions in the market than is wise and, as a result, lose money much more quickly.
facts.claim: Overconfidence leads to positions bigger than is wise, and so to faster losses.

facts.quote: Investors may dismiss downside risks, assuming their analysis or past success guarantees future gains.
facts.claim: Past success can make you assume more gains are coming and wave off the downside.

facts.quote: Acknowledge that luck plays a role in investment outcomes and that success may not always be solely attributed to your skills or knowledge.
facts.claim: Luck plays a part in results; a success is not always all skill.

facts.quote: Overconfidence can also lead to the disposition effect, where investors hold onto losing stocks for too long, expecting them to rebound, while selling winning stocks too early to secure small gains.
facts.claim: The disposition effect, holding losers too long and selling winners too early, is a separate bias that overconfidence can feed.

facts.quote: Maintaining a record of your investment decisions, the reasons behind them, and their outcomes can help you evaluate your past performance and identify areas for improvement.
facts.claim: A journal of decisions, reasons and outcomes helps you judge your real performance.

facts.quote: The house money effect describes investors' tendency to take on more risk with profits from investments than with earned income.
facts.claim: The house money effect: taking more risk with trading profits than with money you earned.

facts.quote: This behavior arises from mental accounting, where investment income is perceived as separate from other earnings.
facts.claim: It comes from mental accounting: treating profit as a separate, lesser kind of money.

facts.quote: The house money effect suggests, for example, that individuals tend to buy higher-risk stocks or other assets after profitable trades.
facts.claim: After profitable trades, people tend to buy riskier stocks.

facts.quote: Letting winners ride in a mathematically calculated position-size strategy is an excellent way of compounding gains.
facts.claim: Growing size by a set, calculated rule is how gains compound, and it is not the house money effect.

facts.quote: While it can sometimes lead to higher returns, it can also cause investors to make careless choices and lose their earlier gains.
facts.claim: Playing with house money can lead to careless choices that give back earlier gains.

facts.quote: The term makes reference to a gambler who takes winnings from previous bets and uses some or all of them in subsequent bets.
facts.claim: The name comes from the casino: a gambler betting the house's money he just won.

facts.quote: too much credit for their own success and do not attribute enough of that success to chance or outside circumstance. Gervais and Odean showed that this bias leads successful investors to become overconfident.
facts.claim: People give themselves too much credit for success and too little to chance or circumstance, and that turns successful investors overconfident.

facts.quote: Research has shown that overconfident investors tend to trade more frequently, resulting in higher transaction costs and increased return volatility.
facts.claim: Overconfident investors trade more often, which raises their costs.

facts.quote: Moreover, overconfident people often underestimate the risks associated with certain investments, leading them to take excessive risks or invest in high-risk assets without properly assessing the potential consequences.
facts.claim: Overconfident people underrate risk and so take too much of it.

facts.quote: Thinking through those decisions before placing a trade by compiling them into a trade plan can help ensure you enter your orders correctly, can potentially help you manage risk
facts.claim: Making the decisions, size included, before the trade and writing them into a plan can help you manage risk.

facts.quote: It also leads us to discount or ignore our mistakes and instead assign blame to others or to things that are outside of our control.
facts.claim: Overconfidence makes us shrug off our mistakes and blame others or things outside our control.

facts.quote: Outcome bias is the tendency to judge a decision by its result rather than the reasoning behind it, putting too much weight on how things turned out.
facts.claim: Outcome bias is judging a decision by how it turned out instead of by its reasoning.

facts.quote: However, a doubling down on a given winning bet exposes him to a single large loss that may wipe out previous gains.
facts.claim: Doubling size after wins exposes you to one large loss that can wipe out the earlier gains.

facts.quote: This type of thinking may fall into the "hot hand fallacy" trap, but when markets are trending up, the anti-Martingale system could be successful for a trader
facts.claim: Sizing up after wins can be the hot hand fallacy, though in a rising market it can work for a while.

facts.quote: It can be effective in strong trending markets, but it can be risky when sudden reversals erase gains and lead to large losses.
facts.claim: Size that grows on wins can work in a strong trend, and a sudden reversal can turn it into large losses.

facts.quote: The 2% rule is a strategy that limits an investor's risk on any single trade to no more than 2% of their total trading capital.
facts.claim: A risk rule is set as a percent of the account: under the 2% rule, at most 2% on any one trade.

facts.quote: Following the 2% rule encourages disciplined decision-making and prevents impulsive trading.
facts.claim: A fixed risk limit exists to stop impulsive decisions.

facts.quote: A good trade plan establishes ground rules for how much you're willing to risk on a single trade.
facts.claim: Your trade plan sets how much you risk on one trade.

facts.quote: For a general rule, some traders may risk up to 1%–2% of their account on a single trade
facts.claim: Risk per trade is set as a percent of the account; Schwab gives up to 1% to 2% as a general rule some traders use.

facts.quote: Were my entries, stops, and exits performed effectively?
facts.claim: Schwab's trade review asks whether your entries, stops and exits were carried out well.

facts.quote: Record your trades in a trading journal.
facts.claim: Keep a trading journal.

facts.quote: track your trading history to calculate your theoretical trade expectancy, meaning your average gain (or loss) per trade.
facts.claim: Your edge is judged over your whole trading history: your average gain or loss per trade.

facts.quote: How did your trade perform relative to your trade plan, portfolio size, and a market benchmark like the S&P 500® index (SPX)?
facts.claim: Judge a trade against your plan and against the market, not on its own.

facts.quote: Of 66,465 households with accounts at a large discount broker during 1991 to 1996, those that trade most earn an annual return of 11.4 percent, while the market returns 17.9 percent.
facts.claim: In 1991 to 1996 the households that traded most earned 11.4% a year; the market returned 17.9%.

facts.quote: Overconfidence can explain high trading levels and the resulting poor performance of individual investors.
facts.claim: Barber and Odean: overconfidence explains the heavy trading and the poor results.

facts.quote: households that trade frequently earn a net annualized geometric mean return of 11.4 percent, and those that trade infrequently earn 18.5 percent.
facts.claim: After costs, the most active households earned 11.4% a year and the least active 18.5%.

facts.quote: In assessing his ability the trader takes too much credit for his successes. This leads him to become overconfident.
facts.claim: Taking too much credit for your wins is how overconfidence builds.

facts.quote: A trader's expected level of overconfidence increases in the early stages of his career. Then, with more experience, he comes to better recognize his own ability.
facts.claim: In the model, overconfidence rises early in a trader's career and eases with experience.

facts.quote: With biased self-attribution, the level of investor overconfidence and thus trading volume varies with past returns.
facts.claim: In overconfidence models with biased self-attribution, overconfidence and trading rise and fall with past returns.

facts.quote: share turnover is positively related to lagged returns for many months
facts.claim: Investors trade more in the months after the market has gone up.

facts.quote: supporting a "house money effect" (increased risk seeking in the presence of a prior gain) and "break-even effects" (in the presence of prior losses, outcomes which offer a chance to break even are especially attractive)
facts.claim: Real-money experiments: after a gain people take more risk; after a loss, a chance to get back to even looks especially good.

facts.quote: to demonstrate a strong positive relationship between prior trading outcomes and subsequent risk taking
facts.claim: Earlier trading results were strongly linked to how much risk traders took next.

facts.quote: investors in this market take above-average risks in afternoon trading after morning gains. The phenomenon is prevalent in all three types of market makers' accounts and across different types of market participants.
facts.claim: On Taiwan's stock index options market, traders with morning gains took above-average risk that afternoon, market makers included.

facts.quote: prospect theory can predict both increased and decreased levels of subsequent risk taking
facts.claim: Theory allows either more or less risk after a gain; these traders took more.

facts.quote: According to their study, active traders underperform the market. Active trading correlates with overconfidence.
facts.claim: In Barber and Odean's study, the most active traders trailed the market, and heavy trading goes with overconfidence.

facts.quote: and succumbing to optimism, short-term thinking, and overconfidence (self-attribution bias)
facts.claim: The report lists overconfidence, in the form of self-attribution bias, among investors' common mistakes.

facts.quote: Investors seemed to have positively biased perceptions of their own knowledge, with almost two-thirds of respondents (64 percent) rating themselves highly (5 to 7 on a 7-point scale).
facts.claim: Most investors, 64%, rated their own investing knowledge highly, and the FINRA Foundation says those self-ratings seemed positively biased.

facts.quote: They perceive themselves as knowledgeable about investing, despite having both fewer correct answers and more incorrect answers on the investor knowledge quiz than those 35 and older.
facts.claim: Younger investors rated themselves knowledgeable while getting more quiz answers wrong than older investors.

facts.quote: In investing, this may cause investors to trust their own predictions more than they should.
facts.claim: Overconfidence makes you trust your own predictions more than you should.

facts.quote: Statman and Thorley (1999) found that over even short horizons, such as a month, current market returns predict subsequent trading volume.
facts.claim: When the market has gone up, investors go on to trade more.

facts.quote: Greater overconfidence leads to greater trading and to lower expected utility.
facts.claim: More overconfidence means more trading and worse outcomes for the trader.

facts.quote: Though a greater number of successes indicates greater probable ability, a more successful trader may actually have lower expected profits in the next period than a less successful trader due to his greater overconfidence.
facts.claim: More wins do hint at more ability, yet in the model the more successful trader can expect lower profits next, because he is more overconfident.

facts.quote: Overconfidence does not make traders wealthier, but the process of becoming wealthy can make traders overconfident.
facts.claim: Overconfidence doesn't make traders rich; getting rich can make them overconfident.

facts.quote: Self-attribution bias is a long-standing concept in psychology research and refers to individuals' tendency to attribute successes to personal skills and failures to factors beyond their control.
facts.claim: Self-attribution bias: crediting your successes to your own skill and blaming your failures on things outside your control.

facts.quote: the higher the returns in a previous period are, the more investors agree with a statement claiming that their recent performance accurately reflects their investment skills
facts.claim: Among real brokerage clients, the better their recent returns, the more they believed those returns reflected their skill.

walkthroughs.title: What a run does to your head
steps: A run of winners feels like proof you've figured it out.
That's self-attribution: the wins are your skill, the losses are bad luck or someone else's fault.
Gervais and Odean show where it leads. Traders take too much credit for their successes and become overconfident.
Overconfidence can show up as bigger positions. And bigger positions lose money faster when you're wrong.

walkthroughs.title: There's no house money
steps: After a gain, people tend to take more risk. Thaler and Johnson called it the house money effect.
It hits pros too. Market makers on Taiwan's index options market took above-average risk after a profitable morning.
Profit is not play money. It's your money, and it follows your normal rules.

walkthroughs.title: Keep the risk flat
steps: Write your risk per trade into your plan before the run starts.
As the account grows, the same percent means more dollars. That's compounding by rule, and it's fine.
What you never do is raise the percent because you feel hot. One oversized loss can wipe out the run.

questions.q: What does overconfidence bias mean?
choices: Overrating your own skill and knowledge
Fearing you'll miss a big move
Holding losers too long to avoid a loss
Buying what everyone else is buying
questions.answer: Overrating your own skill and knowledge
questions.why: Overrating your own skill and knowledge. Investopedia and Schwab define it the same way, and Schwab names where it leads: risky bets and ignored data.
questions.lesson_line: Feeling sure is not the same as being right.

wrong.Fearing you'll miss a big move: That's FOMO, the fear of missing out. Overconfidence is rating yourself too highly.
wrong.Holding losers too long to avoid a loss: That's one half of the disposition effect, a separate bias that also sells winners too soon. Overconfidence can feed it, but the word means overrating yourself.
wrong.Buying what everyone else is buying: That's herd behavior, following the crowd. Overconfidence is trusting your own call too much.

questions.q: In a FINRA Foundation survey, most investors rated their own investing knowledge highly.
questions.why: True. Almost two-thirds, 64 percent, rated themselves highly, and the FINRA Foundation said those self-ratings seemed positively biased.
questions.lesson_line: Overconfidence is common. Assume you have it, and build rules for it.

questions.q: Name the bias.
questions.sentence: Crediting your wins to skill and blaming your losses on bad luck is ___ bias.
questions.why: Self-attribution. The wins become proof of skill and the losses get blamed on things outside your control. A research review done for the SEC lists it as a form of overconfidence.
questions.lesson_line: Grade your wins as hard as you grade your losses.

questions.q: What is the house money effect?
choices: Taking more risk after a gain
Taking more risk after a loss
Selling winners too early
Trading with borrowed money
questions.answer: Taking more risk after a gain
questions.why: Taking more risk after a gain. Thaler and Johnson found it in real-money experiments. The name comes from the casino, where a gambler bets the winnings he just took off the house.
questions.lesson_line: Profit in your account is your money. Risk it like your money.

wrong.Taking more risk after a loss: That's the break-even effect from the same study: grabbing at a chance to get back to even.
wrong.Selling winners too early: That's the disposition effect. House money is about raising your risk after a win.
wrong.Trading with borrowed money: That's margin. The house here is the casino, and the money is a gambler's winnings.

questions.q: A run of winning trades shows your method has gotten better.
questions.why: False. A run can come from luck, or from a strong market lifting most stocks. Wins may hint at some skill, but traders take too much credit for them, and that's how overconfidence builds.
questions.lesson_line: A streak is a result. Your edge shows over your whole record, not a few trades.

questions.q: What best stops your size from creeping up during a hot streak?
choices: A risk % written in your plan
Sizing by how sure you feel
Watching your P&L more closely
Raising size until a loss stops you
questions.answer: A risk % written in your plan
questions.why: A risk % written in your plan. Schwab: a good trade plan sets ground rules for how much you risk on one trade. A fixed limit like the 2% rule exists to stop impulsive trading.
questions.lesson_line: Decide your risk before the streak, so the streak can't decide it for you.

wrong.Sizing by how sure you feel: How sure you feel is exactly what a streak inflates. That's the overconfidence you're guarding against.
wrong.Watching your P&L more closely: Watching the score sets no limit. A fat P&L can make the urge to size up stronger.
wrong.Raising size until a loss stops you: Then the first loss lands at your biggest size. That's how a run gets handed back.

questions.q: In Barber and Odean's study of 66,465 households, how did the ones that traded most do?
choices: Fell short of the market
Beat the market by a bit
Kept pace with the market
questions.why: Fell short of the market. From 1991 to 1996 they earned 11.4% a year after costs, while the market returned 17.9%. The authors say overconfidence can explain the heavy trading.
questions.lesson_line: More trades is not more profit. Every trade has to earn its place.

wrong.Beat the market by a bit: The opposite. The busiest traders trailed: 11.4% a year against the market's 17.9%.
wrong.Kept pace with the market: They fell well short. In the full paper, the least active households netted 18.5% a year and the most active 11.4%.

questions.story: Your plan risks 1% on every trade. You've just closed three winners in a row. The next setup looks great, and you want to risk 3%.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Take it at your usual 1%
Risk 3%, you're seeing it clearly
Risk 2% to meet the urge halfway
questions.why: Take it at your usual 1%. Overconfidence leads to positions bigger than is wise, and those lose money faster. Three wins didn't change your rules.
questions.lesson_line: Your plan sets the risk. Your last three trades don't get a vote.

wrong.Risk 3%, you're seeing it clearly: That's the streak talking. Past success makes you wave off the downside, and one loss at 3% costs three normal losses.
wrong.Risk 2% to meet the urge halfway: That still doubles your risk on a feeling. Meeting the urge halfway is still breaking the plan.

questions.q: Your rule is 1% risk on a $60,000 account. Feeling hot, you set up a trade risking $2,400. How many times your normal risk is that?
questions.why: 4 times. Your normal risk is 1% of $60,000, and $2,400 is four of those. Size creep hides in dollar amounts, so check every trade in percent.
questions.lesson_line: Measure every position against your rule in percent. Dollars can fool you.

questions.q: Risking the same 1% of a bigger account after a good run is oversizing.
questions.why: False. The percent is the rule, and a bigger account turns the same percent into more dollars. Growing size by a set, calculated rule is how gains compound.
questions.lesson_line: Size grows with the account, by rule. It never grows with your mood.

questions.story: Account $50,000, risking 1% a trade. Your last three winners made $500 each. Feeling sure, you risk $2,000 on the next one, and it's stopped out.
questions.q: Where do the four trades leave you?
choices: $500 down
questions.why: $500 down. One stop-out at four times your normal risk took back all three winners, and more. A single large loss can wipe out a run of gains.
questions.lesson_line: Wins come in small steps. One oversized loss can take them all back.

wrong.$1,000 up: That treats the loss like a normal $500 one. It was $2,000, four times that.

questions.story: The market has run up for three months. You notice you're placing about twice as many trades as usual.
questions.q: What do you check first?
choices: Whether each trade met your rules
Whether you can add more names
Whether to raise risk on each one
questions.answer: Whether each trade met your rules
questions.why: Whether each trade met your rules. Research finds investors trade more after the market goes up, and the researchers read it as overconfidence. More trades aren't wrong by themselves, so the test is your rules.
questions.lesson_line: More trades after a run is a flag. Check each one against your rules.

wrong.Whether you can add more names: That feeds the same urge. First find out whether the extra trades came from your rules or your mood.
wrong.Whether to raise risk on each one: That stacks bigger size on top of more trades, both pushed by the same overconfidence.

questions.story: Your last five swing trades all worked. That same month the whole market rallied and most stocks went up.
questions.q: What's the honest read on your run?
choices: The market did a lot of the work
My stock picking jumped a level
Time to size up while it lasts
questions.answer: The market did a lot of the work
questions.why: The market did a lot of the work. People give themselves too much credit for success and too little to chance or outside circumstance, and that's how winners turn overconfident. Take the wins, and let your plan, not the streak, set your size.
questions.lesson_line: In a strong market, compare your results to the market before you grade yourself.

wrong.My stock picking jumped a level: Maybe a little. But wins while most stocks rose can't separate your skill from the market's lift.
wrong.Time to size up while it lasts: That's the hot hand feeling. Size that grows on a run can turn a sudden reversal into a large loss.

questions.story: You're up $4,000 this month. A speculative stock that isn't on your list is ripping. You think: if it fails, I just give back some of this month's gains.
questions.q: What's the trap?
choices: Treating profit as play money
Missing the move by waiting
Risking more than this month's gain
questions.why: Treating profit as play money. That's the house money effect: after profitable trades, people tend to buy riskier stocks. Your $4,000 is yours, and it follows your normal rules.
questions.lesson_line: There's no house money in trading. Profit is just your money.

wrong.Missing the move by waiting: That's FOMO talking. The stock isn't on your list, and this month's profit doesn't change that.
wrong.Risking more than this month's gain: Capping the bet at your gains still treats profit as play money. That mental accounting is how earlier gains get lost.

questions.story: Researchers studied traders on Taiwan's stock index options market, market makers included. Some finished the morning with gains.
questions.q: What did those traders tend to do that afternoon?
choices: Took above-average risk
Cut risk to protect the gain
Traded as they would any day
questions.why: Took above-average risk. Liu and colleagues found it in all three types of market makers' accounts. If market makers do it, assume you will too, unless a rule stops you.
questions.lesson_line: A good morning is not a license to swing bigger in the afternoon.

wrong.Cut risk to protect the gain: Theory allows that, and a good plan might call for it. These traders did the opposite.
wrong.Traded as they would any day: The study found a strong link between earlier results and later risk. The morning's P&L changed how they traded.

questions.q: In Gervais and Odean's model, a trader's overconfidence tends to rise early in a career, then ease with experience.
questions.why: True. The trader takes too much credit for his successes and grows overconfident. With experience, he sees his ability more clearly. The FINRA Foundation saw a similar gap in investors under 35: confident, yet more wrong quiz answers.
questions.lesson_line: Overconfidence doesn't make you rich. Making money can make you overconfident.

questions.q: A friend starts at 100 shares and doubles his size after every win. He wins five in a row. How many shares on trade six?
questions.why: 3,200 shares. Doubling after wins can ride a rising market for a while. But one loss at that size can wipe out the whole run.
questions.lesson_line: Size that doubles on every win can hand the whole streak back in one loss.

questions.story: Your plan risks 1% a trade. In your month-end journal review, you see your risk crept up to 2.5% during a winning streak. Every one of those trades made money.
questions.q: How do you grade the bigger sizing?
choices: A rule break that happened to pay
Fine, since every trade made money
Proof you can handle bigger risk now
questions.answer: A rule break that happened to pay
questions.why: A rule break that happened to pay. Judging a decision by its result instead of its reasoning is outcome bias. Schwab's review checks each trade against your trade plan, not just the P&L.
questions.lesson_line: Grade the decision, not the result. Size that broke the plan is a mistake, win or lose.

wrong.Fine, since every trade made money: That's outcome bias: judging the decision by how it turned out.
wrong.Proof you can handle bigger risk now: A run of wins never tested the bigger size. The first loss at 2.5% does, and it costs two and a half normal losses.

questions.story: It's your best month of the year. Your plan risks more on A+ setups. Lately every setup you look at grades A+.
questions.q: What should you suspect first?
choices: Your wins are inflating your grades
The market is full of A+ setups
Your grading was too strict before
questions.answer: Your wins are inflating your grades
questions.why: Your wins are inflating your grades. Overconfidence makes you trust your own predictions more than you should and underrate the risk. Re-grade each setup against your written checklist.
questions.lesson_line: When every setup looks like an A+, check the grader first.

wrong.The market is full of A+ setups: It might be. But every single one grading A+ right after your best month points at you first.
wrong.Your grading was too strict before: Loosening the grades after a hot run is how size creeps up through the back door.

questions.story: Best quarter you've had. You want to raise risk from 1% to 2% a trade, still within your 2% cap.
questions.q: What would make that a plan and not euphoria?
choices: A rule for it written before the run
It still fits under your 2% cap
You feel sure about the next trades
The quarter's profit covers the risk
questions.answer: A rule for it written before the run
questions.why: A rule for it written before the run. Setting your risk ahead of time is what a trade plan is for. A change made up at your peak is the streak deciding, even under the cap.
questions.lesson_line: Any change in size comes from a rule you wrote while you were calm.

wrong.It still fits under your 2% cap: The cap is a ceiling, not a reason. Jumping to it because the quarter went well is still a mood.
wrong.You feel sure about the next trades: Feeling sure is what a hot run produces, so it can't be the test.
wrong.The quarter's profit covers the risk: That's the house money effect: treating profit as money you can afford to lose.

conflicts: Unit plan hint 'our 2% ceiling from docs/study/sizing_rule.md owner lines': section 1's '2% is the hard ceiling' is not marked as the owner's answer or quoted in his words (the same finding as F9.02's conflicts). So no question asks it as our rule. The 2% appears only as the member's own cap in q20's story and through Investopedia's 2% rule (f24, f25) and Schwab's '1%–2%' (f27). If the owner confirms the 2% ceiling in his own words, q06 and q20 can become house questions.

Unit row 'the four enemies and their antidotes' comes from 06_psychology S4, which is docs/curriculum (never a source). No reliable source for a four-enemies list was found, so the unit teaches the named, sourced biases instead: overconfidence, self-attribution, house money, outcome bias.

Risk after gains: Thaler and Johnson (s7, experiments) and Liu et al. (s8, real trading records) find MORE risk after a gain; Investopedia's 'Avoiding Psychological Mistakes in Investing' says investors limit risk when returns look positive ('protecting the lead'), and Liu et al. note prospect theory can predict either. The file keys only what those two studies observed (q04, q15) and never says everyone takes more risk after a gain.

Scaling up after wins: Investopedia's anti-martingale page (s14) says doubling after wins can work in strong trending markets, and some well-known growth-stock traders raise exposure when they are trading well. The file never keys 'never raise size'. It keys: the percent stays where the plan set it (q08, q10), any change in size comes from a rule written before the run (q20), and doubling on every win carries the risk of one large loss (q17). Checker 2026-11-09: docs/study/sizing_rule.md section 1 (not marked as the owner's answer) has risk chosen by 'your recent performance' among other inputs, and section 5 teaches progressive exposure; both are rules set ahead of time, so the file now says 'change it only by a rule you wrote while calm' (teaches, q20) and q13 says 'let your plan, not the streak, set your size' instead of 'keep the size'.

Barber and Odean (s3, s4) is 1991 to 1996 data with that era's commissions; the paper itself says the gross returns of frequent and infrequent traders differed little, so the gap was mostly the cost of trading. Commissions are lower today. q07 states the numbers as that study's, in its years, and teaches only the overconfidence and overtrading link, not today's size of the gap.

s1 was filed as Tier 1 by the author (commissioned under an SEC agreement, hosted on sec.gov), but its cover says 'The findings do not necessarily reflect the views of the SEC', and it is a Library of Congress literature review, not a rule or primary record. Checker 2026-11-09 refiled it as Tier 2. Every key that cites it (q03, q07, q12) also carries two other Tier 2 publishers that agree, so no key depends on it.

q16: Gervais and Odean's model is about experience (early in a career); FINRA's survey (f46) is about age (younger investors). The why calls the FINRA finding 'something like it', not the same thing. The key rests on the paper's own abstract (f36), which states the model's prediction.

Investopedia's hot hand page notes newer research supports a hot hand in some sports. The file never keys 'the hot hand is never real'; f22 is cited only for the trading-size version, which Investopedia's anti-martingale page calls a possible hot hand fallacy trap.

Self-attribution, two definitions: Investopedia's 'Behavioral Finance' page defines it loosely ('a tendency to make choices based on overconfidence in one's own knowledge or skill'). The file uses the attribution definition: credit for success to yourself, failure to outside forces. It is backed by the SEC-hosted report naming overconfidence as 'self-attribution bias' (f44), Barber and Odean's FAJ article (f15), Investopedia's overconfidence page (f19) and Statman et al. (f37). Gervais and Odean's published article (learningRFS.pdf on Odean's page) states it outright, 'We are prone to attribute success to our own dispositions and failure to external forces', but that PDF's text extracts without spaces, so it is not quoted. Checker 2026-11-09: none of those pages both names the bias and defines both halves, so the checker added Hoffmann and Post (s20, peer-reviewed, Elsevier), whose abstract does (f52), for q03 and w1. The same abstract also finds that 'while individual returns relate to more agreement, market returns have no such effect': belief in skill tracked investors' own returns, not the market's. So the file never says investors credit themselves for MARKET gains; q12 says the trading-volume researchers 'read it as overconfidence', and q13 keys only the honest read of your own run.

Dropped sources (author, 2026-11-09): Investopedia's 'Trading Psychology' (terms/t/trading-psychology.asp) and 'Understanding Attribution Bias in Finance' (attribution-bias-7369317) were read in full with the quote checker's own client (HTTP 200) earlier that day, then refused it (403), plain curl (402) and WebFetch. Their facts were replaced with reachable ones (Barber and Odean's 1999 FAJ article, Investopedia's overconfidence page, Schwab), so no key depends on them. Other Investopedia pages can rate-limit the same way; the quote check found all five used here.

Track audit (2026-11-09, all seven F8 units read together): F8.01 and F8.03 also cited the SEC-hosted report as Tier 1; both now file it as Tier 2 like this unit, under one publisher name, and all three units call it 'a research review done for the SEC' in learner text (q03 here). The q01 wrong note and f07's claim now give the disposition effect both halves, matching F8.03 and F8.04. The house money and break-even effects are taught as mirror images across F8.04 q04 and q04 here, with no clash. No item in this unit was cut.

w1.notes: f44 (SEC-hosted report), f15 (FAJ 1999, authors' copy), f19 and f04 (Investopedia overconfidence, Adam Hayes, updated 2026-07-01) and f35 (RFS abstract) confirmed live in context. Added f52 (Hoffmann and Post 2014) for step 2, which no cited page defined in full. Step 4 softened to 'can show up as' and losses come faster 'when you're wrong' (f04 says 'can lead').

w2.notes: f39 (Thaler and Johnson abstract), f41 (Liu et al. abstract: 'prevalent in all three types of market makers' accounts') and f10 (Investopedia house money, updated 2026-02-24) confirmed live. 'Tend to' keeps the hedge the conflicts note asks for.

w3.notes: f26, f18 (Schwab trade plan, 2024-10-23), f12 (Investopedia: 'mathematically calculated position-size strategy') and f21 (Investopedia anti-martingale) confirmed live in context. 'Never raise the percent because you feel hot' targets feelings, not pre-set rules, so it fits the house sizing rule.

q01.notes: f01 (Investopedia) and f02 (Schwab) confirmed live: two Tier 2 publishers define it alike. Answer is 39 characters, fits the term tile. FOMO, the disposition effect (f07) and herding are real, separate biases; each wrong note is fair. Track audit 2026-11-09: the note on 'Holding losers too long to avoid a loss' called that habit 'the disposition effect', and f07's claim did the same, but the effect has two halves (f07's own quote: hold losers too long 'while selling winning stocks too early'), and F8.03 q03 and F8.04 q04 teach both. Note and claim now name it as one half of the effect; f07 re-read in the quote check that day (found).

q02.notes: f45 confirmed in the FINRA Foundation's December 2022 report (2021 investor survey): 64% rated themselves 5 to 7 of 7, which is most. Changed 'FINRA called those self-ratings positively biased' to 'the FINRA Foundation said those self-ratings seemed positively biased' (the report says 'seemed'), and the lesson 'Overconfidence is the normal setting' to 'Overconfidence is common' (no source says normal).

q03.notes: No cited page both named self-attribution and defined both halves. Added s20/f52 (Hoffmann and Post 2014, peer-reviewed: 'attribute successes to personal skills and failures to factors beyond their control'), confirmed on IDEAS and Maastricht's portal. f44, f15, f19, f37 confirmed live. No other bank word fits the sentence. Track audit 2026-11-09: the why said 'A report prepared for the SEC'; now 'A research review done for the SEC', the one wording the track uses for that report (F8.01, F8.03). Same meaning, f44 unchanged.

q04.notes: f39 (Management Science abstract) and f09, f14 (Investopedia) confirmed live: two publishers agree. The break-even effect (same abstract), the disposition effect and margin are real ideas and wrong here; the notes are fair.

q05.notes: False is right: f35, f50 (wins indicate probable ability but breed overconfidence), f15, f06, f03 confirmed live; the why's 'may hint at some skill' matches f50's hedge. Added f53 (Hoffmann and Post: the better recent returns, the more investors credit their skill).

q06.notes: f26, f18 (Schwab) and f25 (Investopedia 2% rule, James Chen, updated 2026-05-13) confirmed live; '2%' in the why is in f24 and f25. Distractors are real habits: sizing by conviction, watching P&L, pressing until a loss. Plan-set risk is sound trading.

q07.notes: f32, f33 confirmed on the IDEAS abstract, f34 on the authors' copy (Journal of Finance vol. LV no. 2 header), f43 on the SEC-hosted report. 11.4%, 17.9% and 18.5% match. Added 'after costs' (f34: 'net'), since the paper says gross returns of frequent and infrequent traders differed little. flagged-question fix checked 2026-11-11

q08.notes: f04, f05, f25 (Investopedia) and f26 (Schwab) confirmed live. Recomputed: 3% / 1% = three normal losses; 2% / 1% doubles. A plan that says 1% on every trade stays at 1% on a feeling; the conflicts note covers rule-based scaling.

q09.notes: Recomputed: 1% of $60,000 = $600; $2,400 / $600 = 4; calc matches. f26, f24, f04 confirmed live.

q10.notes: False is right: the same percent of a bigger account is the calculated sizing f12 describes ('mathematically calculated position-size strategy ... compounding gains', read in its house money context). f24 and f27 confirmed live.

q11.notes: Recomputed: 3 x $500 = $1,500; $1,500 - $2,000 = -$500; calc matches. Normal risk is 1% of $50,000 = $500, so $2,000 is four times. Rewrote the unclear '$1,000 up' note ('only nets out when every trade risks the same') to 'treats the loss like a normal $500 one'. f21, f04, f27 confirmed.

q12.notes: f38 (Statman et al., RFS abstract) and f48 (Barber and Odean, FAJ) confirmed live: two publishers agree trading rises after market gains. Changed the cause 'as credit for the gains feeds overconfidence' to 'the researchers read it as overconfidence' (Statman et al. 'interpret' it so; Hoffmann and Post find market returns alone do not raise belief in skill, see conflicts). Keeps the fair caveat that more trades are not wrong by themselves.

q13.notes: f15, f35, f06, f31, f22, f23 confirmed live. Changed 'Take the wins and keep the size' to 'let your plan, not the streak, set your size' (the house sizing rule lets a pre-set plan vary risk with performance), and the hot-hand note to 'can turn' (f23 says 'can be risky').

q14.notes: f11, f10, f13 (Investopedia) and f39 (Thaler and Johnson) confirmed live. Was leading: the story spelled out 'it's only profit' and a distractor said 'profit is there to bet'. Rewrote the thought ('if it fails, I just give back some of this month's gains') and swapped that distractor for 'Risking more than this month's gain', a real house money mistake.

q15.notes: f40, f41, f42 confirmed on the Liu et al. abstract (Management Science 2010); f11 (Investopedia) agrees on the direction. Softened 'If professionals do it, you will too' to 'If market makers do it, assume you will too'.

q16.notes: f36 matches the RFS abstract word for word; f51 on Odean's page; f46 in the FINRA report. Split the run-on sentence; 'FINRA' made 'the FINRA Foundation' and pinned to f46's under-35 group, called 'a similar gap' since the model is about experience and FINRA about age.

q17.notes: Recomputed: 100 doubled five times = 3,200 shares on trade six; calc matches. f21, f22, f23 confirmed live. Split a 23-word sentence in the why (22 is the limit).

q18.notes: f20 (Investopedia outcome bias, updated 2026-10-06) and f31, f28 (Schwab) confirmed live: two publishers. Recomputed: 2.5% / 1% = two and a half normal losses.

q19.notes: f47, f17, f05 (Investopedia) and f02 (Schwab) confirmed live. 'Suspect first' is hedged, and the 'market is full of A+ setups' note concedes it might be; sound trading sense.

q20.notes: Story and key contradicted each other ('You decide' at the peak, keyed 'It was written down before the run'). Rewrote to 'You want to raise risk', 'What would make that a plan', key 'A rule for it written before the run', which matches the house sizing rule's pre-set inputs. f18, f26, f25, f05, f12 confirmed live.
